children: Microfinance institutions (MFIs) are expanding into MSME lending, loans against property, vehicle finance and gold loans as they diversify beyond traditional group lending, nearly a year after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) eased asset exposure norms for the sector.

The regulatory change, which reduced the minimum share of qualifying microfinance assets from 75 per cent to 60 per cent of the total portfolio, has given lenders greater flexibility to build non-microfinance businesses and lower concentration risks arising from overdependence on a single borrower segment.
The move came after stress in the microfinance sector highlighted the risks of excessive exposure to a narrow customer base, with rising delinquencies impacting asset quality across the industry.

Since the change, several MFIs have begun leveraging their branch networks, customer relationships and underwriting capabilities to enter secured and higher-ticket lending segments, including MSME loans, housing-related finance and gold-backed credit.

“We have added products in the MSME space. Initially, we were doing only ₹5 lakh to ₹15 lakh. Now we have increased our ticket size from ₹5 lakh to ₹50 lakh,” said Sanjay Garyali, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Fusion Finance.

Fusion Finance has sharpened its focus on MSME lending as part of its diversification strategy. The company has expanded its ticket size in the segment and introduced new products aimed at higher-value borrowers.
The lender, traditionally focused on Joint Liability Group (JLG) loans, has also launched a prime JLG product for customers seeking loans above ₹3 lakh, he added.

Meanwhile, Aarohan Financial Services is evaluating multiple new business lines, including loans against property, home improvement finance, vehicle financing and gold loans. The company expects one of these segments to be selected for launch after board approvals.

“Between these four areas where preparatory work has been done, with the guidance of the board, we will decide on one and move ahead with the launch,” said Manoj Nambiar, Managing Director of Aarohan Financial Services.

Nambiar said MFIs are likely to keep their core microfinance operations at around 65 per cent of their portfolio, while gradually increasing the share of non-microfinance assets. Aarohan currently has about 68 per cent of its portfolio in microfinance loans, he added.

Fusion Finance has set a more aggressive diversification goal, aiming to increase the share of non-microfinance assets to 30-35 per cent over the next two years from around 14 per cent currently. The company plans to utilise branches located in MSME-heavy markets to expand lending with only a limited increase in operating costs.

Some lenders entered the transition with diversified business models already in place. Satin Creditcare Network for instance, said its existing presence in non-qualifying assets and alternative investment businesses has helped it adapt smoothly to the revised framework.
“Diversification has panned out better for us. We were diversified even before the RBI circular,” said a senior company officials during the lender’s quarterly earnings interaction.

Industry executives, however, expect diversification to be gradual, given the intense competition from established players in segments such as MSME, vehicle and gold lending. Expanding into new businesses also requires investments in products, talent and distribution capabilities, making execution a key challenge for MFIs navigating the transition.

title: MFIs foray into MSME, Gold Loans as RBI eases portfolio restrictions
